\chapter{Synthesis --- Sentences Worth Saying}
\label{ch:synthesis-relative}
\hlchaptermodality{181}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can build a sentence containing other sentences.}

Complete ES-C53-sintesis-frases-largas: build a three-verb sentence and say why length is not difficulty.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Synthesis — sentences worth saying}

\label{lesson:ES-C53-sintesis-frases-largas}



\begin{quote}
Until this rung, every sentence you could build had one verb in it. Count the verbs in the next one.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{The exchange}
\begin{quote}
— \emph{¿Tienes el libro \textbf{que} compré?} — \emph{Sí. \textbf{Lo que} no tengo es la comida \textbf{que} haces.}
\end{quote}

Read the second line again. It has three verbs in it, and you can build every piece of it:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{lo que no tengo} — the thing I do not have \emph{(a noun-shaped hole)}
  \item \emph{es} — is
  \item \emph{la comida que haces} — the meal you make \emph{(a noun with a sentence hung off it)}
\end{itemize}

Nothing in that sentence is new. What is new is that the pieces are allowed to sit \textbf{inside} each other.

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: length is not difficulty}]
Long sentences look like an increase in difficulty and are not.

A relative clause does not add grammar. It adds a \textbf{slot} where a whole sentence can go, and you fill it with the same Spanish you were already making. Two short sentences become one long one, and the only new thing is the joint.

That is why this is the last structural rung a beginner's course owes you. Not because nothing is left, but because from here the growth is \textbf{more of what you have}, arranged more deeply. What remains genuinely hard is vocabulary and hearing speed, and both are time.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the full two-line exchange
  \item the long sentence broken into its three pieces, then whole
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How many verbs can one sentence hold now? (\textbf{As many as you can join.}) What does a relative clause actually add? (A \textbf{slot}, not new grammar.) And what is genuinely hard from here? (\textbf{Vocabulary and hearing speed} — both of which are time.)
\end{tcolorbox}
